The European bloc is stepping up some of its efforts in the resource-rich region, but says it still wants fossil fuels to stay in the ground
The European Commission has presented an updated strategy for the Arctic as climate change and rapidly melting ice open up the remote but resource-rich region.
“With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition,” said European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday.
With the new strategy, the commission aims for the EU to keep pace with rivals as new shipping routes and mining opportunities, including for critical raw materials, become available.
“Access to Arctic sea lanes and natural resources is of strategic interest to the EU,” Kallas said.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500 rise, Nasdaq slips as investors await SpaceX, Netflix earnings
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500 rise, Nasdaq slips as investors await SpaceX, Netflix earnings
articles.content_orig:
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
In a previous life, when I routinely shut down New York City bars, the end of Daylight Saving Time was an annual bonus, as 2am on a Saturday night instantly became 1am, leaving three more hours until closing time.
The financial markets now are undergoing several forms of late-cycle unease, and Wall Street is now looking for earnings season and the passage of the midterm elections to turn back the clock before last call.
To be clear, this remains a bull market, the S&P 500 's uptrend unbroken, with constant rotations between AI tech and remainder of the market fitfully supporting the tape, with pullbacks limited to 3% for half a year.
Still, the index is now chopping around a flattish 50-day moving average at levels first reached 11 weeks ago, the AI-hardware cohort has badly broken stride, bank stocks are trading poorly off their results, and credit markets are getting colicky.
Late last week, the urgent selling in semiconductors and data-center equities and debt resembled the sort of forced-unwind rhythms from July, when a big upstart tech hedge fund was in the process of being all but liquidated.
A tentative bounce in semiconductor stocks Monday was minimally reassuring, in that it meant we didn't get the further disorderly purge many had braced for over the weekend (when S&P 500 "perpetual" futures on Hyperliquid had a sudden head-fake drop late Saturday).
Jason Hunter, technical strategist at JP Morgan, sets out the crucial question for a market sending mixed signals:
"With the bearish seasonal window now closing, we are left wondering if the market is in the terminal phase of a sequence of rolling corrections ahead of a typical late-year rally. Or are the plentiful amounts of bearish internal, momentum, and intra-market divergences that have formed as the S&P 500 index has decelerated below longer-term channel resistance setting the market up for a larger and more correlated setback?"
He leans toward a more cautious interpretation, keeping the S&P 500 on a short leash that extends about 2.5% lower to 7500, a break of which would lose the tape the benefit of the doubt.
Based on precedent and circumstance, the market "should" be setting up for a comeback that could reset the clock in bulls' favor. The fourth quarter after a midterm election year, historically, is overwhelmingly positive. Earnings growth projected to exceed a 20% year-over-year growth rate again this quarter can hardly be viewed as anything but a positive at least to bolster the fundamental case.
Still, against most probabilities, 2018 happened. By which I mean a 19% S&P 500 peak-to-trough decline in the fourth quarter of a midterm-election year, one that saw total S&P 500 earnings grow by more than 20%.
The 2018 tailspin had followed a massive momentum crescendo and reversal several months earlier, which gave way to an erratic tape that couldn't absorb what seemed at the time relatively unthreatening Federal Reserve tightening actions.
Financial conditions have now been tightening by means of higher Treasury yields, somewhat wider corporate-credit spreads, an uptick in volatility and a stronger U.S. dollar.
It's become common to hear investors insist that "the market is doing the Fed's tightening for it," suggesting Chairman Kevin Warsh himself should show restraint in further hiking rates despite the recent upturn in inflation. Sure, but the reason the markets are tightening is, in part, because Warsh himself expressed resolve in fighting inflation and investors therefore believe he'll take short-term rates up a bit more.
How Warsh treats these market shifts after next week's Fed meeting is another node of disagreement on the Street.
Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave says the markets are testing the Fed's pain threshold with the Nasdaq retreating 5% and credit spreads flaring a bit. The market has taken recent Fedspeak to suggest very low chances of an October rate hike, even though Warsh himself has decried forward guidance and said the Fed shouldn't suppress normal market volatility. Bhave is maintaining his non-consensus prediction for an October hike, conceding it's a close call.
Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson takes the other side on the Fed's response to the recent tensing up of markets: "We think some acknowledgement of this tightening by Warsh would be well received by rate-sensitive areas that have already derated notably. Conversely, an indifference to this tightening may invoke memories of Powell's 2018 'auto-pilot' remarks in reference to that tightening episode."
The "de-rating" and "de-risking" process has surely been notable in recent weeks, with small and cyclical stocks under significant valuation pressure and hedge funds aggressively repositioning out of tech.
Is it enough to enliven buyers into or after the election?
Ned Davis Research thematic strategist Pat Tschosik notes his firm's proprietary market-breadth reading Big Mo Tape tentatively turning higher from oversold readings. "If Big Tech disappoints on Q3 earnings, we may get a full market washout and Big Mo could head even lower like it did in October 2023. Perhaps this is what is needed to set up for a post-midterm-election rally into yearend."
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors sees a similar level to JPMorgan's as the market's breaking point, while evaluating his sentiment indicator.
Kolovos on the latest reading: "A noticeable sentiment reset is underway on the heels of the AI trade unwind and tightening financial conditions.  The good news is that bullish sentiment is finally starting to wash out, which should set the stage for a year-end rally. However, a break below the mid-September lows on the S&P 500 near 7,500 would warn that something more than a routine pullback is unfolding."
-There's something of a paradox at work – or a collective investor blind spot - when the bond market is finally offering relatively safe income after many years of meager yields and yet people continue to rush for the engineered income delivered by options-selling ETFs. This CNBC.com piece offers a thorough, smart rundown of these strategies, complete with warnings of tax pitfalls. This Bloomberg report details a more aggressive approach through funds many investors don't quite understand, while introducing me to the community of self-styled "dividend nomads."
-Anthropic's proposal to place 5% of its equity into a "public benefit fund" to help groups potentially disadvantaged by AI's propagation and Elon Musk's stated offer to give one of his SpaceX shares to every American child via Trump Accounts suggest that anxiety over AI economic disruption is going from simmer to boil.
We can cynically observe that such efforts also hype these companies' world-changing potency, a form of marketing through scare-mongering sheathed in generosity.  But the concern over AI's impact on current worker groups is well-placed, even if ultimately society adapts around step-function technological change. The best hedge against AI-powered capital overtaking labor is arguably to own more capital, whether through the S&P 500 or other vehicles.
Or one could raise the value of one's human capital, through training or becoming excellent at something. This has always been Warren Buffett's answer for how one should become inflation-resistant, as he detailed at Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting a few years ago , at the height of the pandemic inflation surge.
Bull markets can keep rolling for a long while after they've become fully embraced and stocks are no longer cheap. But I find myself cataloguing various ways that the cushions against adverse surprises are getting worn pretty flat.
Here's the running tally of investors' collective cash holdings as a percentage of total margin debt. It's running well below the levels of the year 2000 at this point.

articles.title_orig: Woke French student mocked owners who lost stores in riots — then her jet-set life was revealed: ‘Your little shops, that’s cute’
articles.title_zh: Woke French student mocked owners who lost stores in riots — then her jet-set life was revealed: ‘Your little shops, that’s cute’
articles.content_orig:
By AIDAN RADNEDGE, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER
Published: 07:01 EDT, 20 October 2026 | Updated: 12:25 EDT, 20 October 2026
The BBC has been mocked for describing the France riots as 'mostly peaceful' as background footage showed Paris in flames and masked thugs battling police.
A report on the corporation's flagship News At Ten, covering the weekend of nationwide rioting and looting , has been accused by some viewers of downplaying the carnage.
The coverage from the French capital on Sunday night's show included the BBC's Paris correspondent, James Waterhouse, describing the protests as 'mostly peaceful'.
His words came as a voiceover to footage of fights in the streets between masked thugs and police, fires, explosions and looters attacking a wine shop.
Demonstrations began over the cost-of-living crisis, education standards and President Emmanuel Macron 's government, but they swiftly descended into anarchy.
Several cities, including Paris, have now banned protests while the government considers declaring a state of emergency.
Waterhouse, speaking on Sunday's News At Ten, said: 'In Paris and beyond, half a million people had filled cities across France to protest over the future of their country.
'They were mostly peaceful, but as we saw in the capital, in the wings were those who wanted to take advantage of the disorder.
The BBC's Paris correspondent James Waterhouse filed a report on the riots engulfing the country for Sunday's News At Ten, calling the protests 'mostly peaceful'
The backdrop was footage of carnage, including street fires such as this one in the heart of Paris at the Place de la Republique
'The shops that have been hit have been completely gutted, like this wine shop has been looted top to bottom.
'And this morning, in Paris and across France, there is an anger – few believe this was at the hands of the genuine protesters, but down to an opportunistic minority who came in and sought to rob and cause carnage.'
Viewers have questioned the phrasing, with some accusing the corporation of playing down the extent of the widespread chaos and how many violent offenders were taking part.
Writer and broadcaster Emma Trimble posted: 'If it were not for social media, we would have no idea what is going on in France. The BBC are still claiming it is "mostly peaceful".'
Another wrote: 'Mostly peaceful protests is how the BBC described the unrest in France. Another narrative to gaslight millions.'
Comments on the BBC News channel on YouTube, underneath the video shared, included: 'Mostly Peaceful... Lets ignore the looting, burning down of buildings, cars, and bikes on the street.'
Another viewer said: 'How can a state broadcaster possibly say any of the above was "mostly peaceful" – this is utter nonsense.'
Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, whose party wants to scrap the licence fee, said: 'The BBC is broken. Calling the riots in France "mostly peaceful" tells you everything you need to know.'
Others took issue with how the 19th century town hall in Limoges was described as 'badly damaged' by News At Ten presenter Jane Hall after it was engulfed in flames and collapsed on Saturday, with one viewer responding: 'That town is completely destroyed, not damaged.'
The report that followed told how the building was 'devoured by flames'.
Do YOU think the violence in France was downplayed?
Burning cars, ransacked shops and street battles involving rioters were shown
The 19th century town hall in Limoges was set ablaze, with its belltower and belfry collapsing
Jane Hill on Sunday night's edition of the BBC's News At Ten described the town hall as 'badly damaged'
Police officers clashed with protesters in the French capital on Saturday
A man taking part in the protests that turned into riots runs past a burning car in Paris
A rioter films himself as he uses an iron bar to smash the window of an Adidas store at Châtelet-Les Halles in Paris on Sunday
Sunday night's report from Paris featured interviews with victims of the violence, including owners of shops that had been ransacked and a woman who was injured, who believed she had been hit in the face with an iron bar.
A BBC spokesperson said: 'No one watching, reading or listening to BBC News coverage of the France protests and riots can be in any doubt as to what was happening – there is coverage of the fires, the looting and violence.
'James Waterhouse and the team of reporters in France over the weekend gave broader context to the protests and riots – making the point that, as well as the destructive scenes, several hundred thousand people were on the streets in peaceful protest, and those carrying out the violence and looting were a small fraction of that number.'
About 2,400 people were arrested over the weekend and authorities said thousands of businesses were damaged or looted.
President Emmanuel Macron denounced what he called 'unrestrained violence' by 'insurrectionist elements from radical far-Left groups, joined by numerous criminals'.
Paris police issued an overnight curfew on Monday in two areas of the French capital aimed at protecting 'people and property from the violence and looting', the city's police said in a statement.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had earlier called for 'very limited' and 'localised' curfews.
He said in a post on X today: 'The targeted curfews have contributed to the calm of last night.'
He added that such measures could be extended 'where the situation requires it'.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war
articles.title_zh: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
A second source involved in the matter in Israel confirmed Tuesday morning that Netanyahu met Hegseth.
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Hegseth confirmed the visit in comments to reporters Tuesday, saying he "was there visiting our troops" and "had a chance to talk to the prime minister."
"Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about but they've been good partners and I appreciate that," Hegseth said.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit. CBS News has reached out to the Israeli government for comment.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.
Israeli and U.S. forces jointly launched strikes against Iran in late February, and the two allies worked closely with each other early in the war. The U.S. also struck three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during a broader conflict between Israel and Iran.
Iran and the U.S. have largely refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, but Mr. Trump has said openly that he is still weighing whether to cut a deal with Iran's leadership or "annihilate" the country — a decision he says could come after the November midterm elections .
Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, faces his own political uncertainty a week from Tuesday. The coalition led by his right-wing Likud party is seeking to remain in power, but it faces several more centrist challengers, including one party run by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu told Israeli media last week he is not planning to launch renewed strikes against Iran before the Oct. 27 elections, saying , "it is not convenient for us."
Mr. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday , calling him "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
The U.S. president has maintained a close relationship with Netanyahu, though he has put pressure on Israel at times. Over the spring and summer, the Trump administration urged Israel to ease up on striking Lebanon, home to Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.
The administration has also encouraged Israel to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank and cut a longer-term deal with Hamas in the Gaza Strip.
Last month, Trump envoy Jared Kushner suggested the upcoming Israeli elections may have delayed progress in Gaza, saying at a conference in Kyiv: "They just have a crazy election, and that makes them a little irrational in certain regards."
Michal  Ben-Gal , Charlie  D'Agata and Eleanor  Watson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
articles.title_zh: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
articles.content_orig:
By REBECCA ENGLISH, ROYAL EDITOR and KATHERINE LAWTON, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER
Published: 14:07 EDT, 20 October 2026 | Updated: 17:00 EDT, 20 October 2026
The Prince and Princess of Wales dazzled at King Charles 's state banquet for the Sultan of Oman tonight - just hours after Prince Harry's interview insisting he wants to reconcile with his family.
The monarch was accompanied by William and Catherine, Queen Camilla , the Princess Royal and her husband Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence , as well as the Duke and Duchess of Gloucester as they hosted Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said and his retinue in St George's Hall at Windsor Castle.
Kate wore an ethereal pale yellow Ellie Saab gown with a cape detail and train, which she paired with her favourite Lover's Knot tiara, diamond earrings and a bracelet belonging to the late Queen Elizabeth.
William was dressed for the occasion in a white tie with the Windsor tail coat, his Most Noble Order of the Garter Sash with the Lesser George and other medals and decorations.
Camilla looked regal in a purple chiffon dress by Fiona Clare, while Charles sported the Sash of the Order of Al Said, an honour given to him by the Sultan of Oman earlier in the day.
One hundred and sixty guests were invited to dine on Scottish langoustine and Cornish crab, pot roasted Windsor pheasant and stuffed cabbage, individual baked Alaskas with Balmoral Plum and Windsor Estate honey ice cream.
It came hours after the King's youngest son Harry insisted he wants to reconcile with his family , while denying he was taking a 'swipe' at his brother William when declaring: 'Some people don't want it to work out.'
The Duke of Sussex , who has not spoken to William for four years, admitted in an interview with GQ that he is grieving his 'complicated relationships' with the King and the Prince of Wales.

Charles spoke tonight of the importance of the friendship between Britain and Oman at a time of 'painful' conflict in the Middle East.
And amid the continuing drama around Harry, he told the Sultan of Oman of his pride that both 'our sons' - William and the Crown Prince of Oman - had become joint patrons of the Jewel of Arabia expedition, a cultural and environmental trek through the region last year.
'Your Majesty, there can be few happier symbols of success than a living relationship being passed from one generation to the next,' he said.
His speech came at the end of a damp but successful day as the Sultan arrived at Windsor Castle at the start of a three-day State Visit.
Oman is one of Britain's oldest and most trusted allies in Arabia and the British government requested the state visit to emphasise trade, military and cultural links at a perilous time in the region.
Toasting his guests at the banquet, Charles said it was a 'treasured moment to receive dear and old friends'.
'Oman is one of Britain's oldest allies and, after all these years, I pray, one of your closest friends,' he said.
He said he had been 'immensely fortunate and blessed' to have come to know Oman well over many visits and praised both the late Sultan's 'inspired leadership' and the present leader's 'energetic and far-sighted leadership'.
Turning to the current conflict, he said: 'I would especially like to recognise, at a time when conflict has returned so painfully to the region, Oman's enduring commitment as a trusted interlocutor to all parties.'
And referring to the Strait of Hormuz he said: 'Oman's noble efforts in trying to keep open one of the world's most important shipping routes have been of great service to the whole international community, and particularly to the most vulnerable of those affected.
'Oman's role across the Gulf and her 'constructive neutrality', as you put it, matters far beyond Hormuz, and is worthy of our utmost respect.
'The unique and special relationship we share helps to make the world and our peoples safe.'
The King also highlighted the environmental challenges facing both countries and the 'promise and peril' of AI.
He concluded: 'Your Majesty, I hope this State Visit shows the importance the United Kingdom attaches to Oman, its monarchy and institutions, and to our friendship with you personally. '
King Charles poses before the state banquet for the Sultan of Oman tonight

The King Charles III cypher imprinted into salt on the banquet table this evening
Tonight's 50 metre long table, which runs the whole length of the room, was laid with 480 knives, 480 forks, 160 spoons and the Grand Service, commissioned by George IV, which runs to more than 4,000 silver-gilt pieces.
In a touching tribute, the centre 12-light St George and the dragon candelabra, commissioned by William IV in 1833, was decorated with pomegranates grown on a tree planted by the late Duke of Edinburgh around 50 years ago on the East Terrace.
The unseasonably warm summer has caused it to fruit so staff decided to use them as decorations, although they are not not be consumed afterwards as they are inedible.
For the first time the salt on the table has been imprinted with the King's royal cypher.
Among the guests are athlete Mazoon Al Alawi and sailor Mohsin Al Busaidi. It is also Andy Burnham's first state banquet as Prime Minister.
It comes after Charles rolled out a rather soggy red carpet earlier today as senior royals welcomed the Sultan - described as one of the world's 'most discreet billionaires' - to the castle for his State Visit.
Tonight, the King has served up a cocktail inspired by an Omani ritual meaning 'hospitality'.
The post-state banquet drink is based on a spiced coffee traditionally shared in Oman, with dates as a gesture of friendship, and has been 'reimagined' by the team at Windsor Castle .
The beverage has been adapted through a 'distinctly British lens', drawing on the nation's long-standing love of tea while preserving the aromatic spices and flavours that make Kahwa so distinctive: fragrant cardamom, delicate rose, sweet dates, and gentle warming spices.
These notes have been woven together with British teas and Windsor honey for a non-alcoholic treat.
Guests were invited to choose from an Iced Earl Grey & Date, an Iced Mint & Rose, or a Warm Cardamom-Spiced Blend sweetened with Windsor Honey.
One hundred and sixty guests have been invited to dine on Scottish langoustine and Cornish crab
Cutlery on the grand table for tonight is the castle's finest
Tonight's flower selection included handpicked seasonal flowers from the gardens at Buckingham Palace.
During Harry's interview today, the Duke was asked directly whether he really wanted to heal the rift with his brother and father. Harry replied: 'Of course I do. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile. That's the key point.'
But in remarks widely interpreted as a dig at William, he added: 'Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out.'

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to meet with U.S. special envoys on Tuesday after U.S. President Donald Trump aimed a fresh spate of criticism at the wartime leader.
Zelenskyy will arrive in Norway on Tuesday and meet with the country's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr and President of Finland Alexander Stubb in Oslo later in the day. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will also take part in the discussions.
The meetings come as tensions mount between Zelenskyy and Trump, while the U.S. has recently eased some pressure on Russia, which invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Ukraine requested that Witkoff and Kushner join the meeting in Oslo, Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement.
"Diplomatic efforts have previously taken place in several countries, and Norway and Finland are pleased to be able to continue this work. The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," he said.
Trump responded to criticism on Monday that he waived sanctions against Russia recently and is on the "wrong side" of history .
"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said to reporters outside the White House. "Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago."
"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump said, echoing previous calls for a "new president" in Kyiv. "If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he'd have a million people living from his side."
Trump also said he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to figure out how to end the Ukraine war, which reportedly could exclude Zelenskyy. "Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said.
Last week, Zelenskyy hit out at the U.S. government over restrictions on access to satellite services offered by SpaceX 's military satellite system, Starshield, which is critical to Ukraine's defense against Russian strikes.
"No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," Zelenskyy said on Monday.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had shifted the blame to the U.S. government and Trump, who he said are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the U.S. is responsible, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Zelenskyy to be "very careful about making statements like this that aren't true."
Trump said Monday that he doesn't know who restricted the Starlink service in Ukraine, "but I'd like to find out."
— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger has contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Dear Tim Sweeney, You Could Learn A Thing Or Two From The Xbox Exec Who Posted So Bad That He Had To Delete His Account
articles.title_zh: Dear Tim Sweeney, You Could Learn A Thing Or Two From The Xbox Exec Who Posted So Bad That He Had To Delete His Account
articles.content_orig:
A better world is possible
In the relatively short time since we launched Aftermath, we’ve watched the world change markedly as generative AI and authoritarianism have reshaped a landscape that was already full of fissures. Through it all, we have held firm in one core value: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney should log off .
I bring this up because now we’ve even found him a potential role model: Xbox senior business strategy manager Brandon Stirrup. We’re talking about a man molded in Sweeney’s own image—at least, as far as posting goes—but with one crucial distinction: Stirrup ultimately logged off.
He began his posting spree over the weekend, boasting that he’d "vibe coded a bad but improvable game" and that “anyone can build a game.” This gave way to multiple diatribes about how generative AI is the de facto future of game development.
"Look if I'm fired tomorrow it will be because I told you the truth that nobody wants you to know,” he wrote on Sunday. “You can make a game with a simple prompt and yes you can make custom, tailored games. Everything you want in a game is right there for the taking, for better or worse. … I’m happy to take the hit if it means hundreds at Xbox can stop pretending that they’re not using AI. It’s time to accept and move forward.”
Never mind that it is extremely well known that some developers who work at Microsoft-owned studios are using AI. Going into Monday, Stirrup still had more golden wisdom to share. He tweeted:
Then, yesterday evening, something resembling common sense stirred up in Stirrup, and he deleted his Twitter account. An Xbox source told PC Gamer he did so because of “the volume of replies he was receiving.”
This, to me, is the platonic ideal of a Bad Poster, the example all others should follow. You say some dumb bullshit, dig your heels in for a while, get absolutely obliterated in the replies, and then delete your account. Stirrup even did us a favor by speedrunning the whole process. Fantastic. No notes.
Tim Sweeney, I’m begging you: learn from this. You’re never gonna beat Stirrup’s time, but you can still log off whenever you want. I guarantee it’ll be better than the elaborate series of humiliation rituals that has become your life.

articles.title_zh: Russia is working 'closely' with Iran as Qatar says US-Tehran talks are still on
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump warned President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday of consequences if he refuses to negotiate an end to the war with Russia, arguing that the U.S. has spent billions on Ukraine only to get "grief” in return.
"What's happening is that Russia would like to get it done," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, describing Russia as a "big machine" that just keeps "grinding forward."
"They've taken a very large piece of land. And you know, you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week. It's just, they march forward.
"Ukraine has to want to settle this war. Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war.
"And if he doesn't, I think it's going to be a very bad thing," Trump warned, arguing that the U.S. has received little in return for its billions of dollars in aid to Kyiv.
"But we gave $350 billion to Ukraine. And, you know, I insisted on getting something for that money.
"And we got a very big chunk of land and rare earth and other things if anybody remembers. Let's see what that amounts to," he said, adding that the U.S. "got nothing back other than high diesel."
"We have, we have given probably possibly more money to Ukraine than almost anybody over the years, hundreds of billions of dollars. And the American taxpayers are tired of it.
"We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” he said.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Tuesday that he made an visited Israel on Monday and met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"I was there visiting our troops," Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisconsin.
"Had a chance to talk to the Prime Minister. Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about, but they've been good partners and I appreciate that."
Hegseth’s remarks follow reports that the high-level meeting took place at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel.
According to sources, the private talks centered heavily on regional security concerns, including threats posed by Iran .
Hegseth also met with U.S. service members stationed in the region under U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM).
Fox News' Liz Friden contributed to this report.
Tehran rejected a U.S. arrest warrant targeting former Cuban President Raul Castro on Tuesday, labeling the move an illegal and criminal act of foreign intervention.
In an official statement, the Iranian Foreign Ministry also denounced U.S. economic sanctions and intimidation tactics against Cuban officials, framing Washington's pressure campaign as a violation of the U.N. Charter and international law.
Tehran also reiterated its solidarity with the Cuban government, Iran International reported.
The statement followed an arrest warrant filed by Florida prosecutors charging Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
The charges stem from his role as defense minister during the 1996 shootdown of two civilian planes operated by the exile group Brothers to the Rescue, which left four people dead.
Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, met with Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, on Tuesday and said Tehran would not surrender any enriched uranium or negotiate with the U.S. until Washington rebuilt trust and met Iran's conditions.
“Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran,” Rezaei later said in a post on X .
“There will be no negotiations until the United States takes steps to build trust,” he added, saying the process must begin with the “full fulfillment of all Iran’s conditions.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio accused Iran on Tuesday of attacking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz and targeting civilian crews — tactics he compared to Nazi U-boat operations during World War II.
“You haven’t seen that since the Second World War. They are doing Nazi U-boat tactics,” Rubio told India's Network18, according to Iran International .
Rubio also warned that a diplomatic solution with Tehran would be difficult because Iran is governed by "radical Shia clerics."
Rubio added that Washington would maintain “extraordinary economic pressure” to cut off funding for Tehran's regional proxies and military production.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that hatred between President Vladimir Putin and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is a major obstacle to ending the war in Ukraine, arguing that Zelenskyy could have secured a better peace deal two years ago.
“We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
“He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office.
“We had a now quite well remembered chat with JD, myself, some others.
“ Zelenskyy could have made a good deal then, could have made a much better deal then probably possibly than he could make now.
“But he's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it.
“What it affects me is to see that many souls lost so needlessly,” he added.
“The hatred between President Putin and President Zelenskyy is tremendous,” Trump said.
“I think that's most of the reason they haven't been able to make a deal, actually," he added.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that military strikes against Iran are not enough unless the United States can ensure the country will not develop a nuclear weapon in the years ahead.
“When people are unhappy with the gasoline. I hate to sound trivial, but, they say it themselves. It's a it's a big price, but actually, it's a small price to pay for not letting Iran have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
“And they will never have a nuclear weapon. We could leave right now, and we would have done a good job, a great job, that that beautiful plane right there took them out.”
“But it's under hundreds of tons of rock. But it's not good enough for me,” Trump added.
“We have to make sure it doesn't happen in five years, six years, 10 years.”
“And that's what's going to happen. So it really is. It's a very small price to pay for not letting the most dangerous country in the world have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said the country has established a 700-square-kilometer security zone in southern Lebanon as part of a new strategy to protect northern Israel from Hezbollah threats.
Katz also said the Israeli military has no plans to leave southern Lebanon anytime soon.
"The IDF will not move out of the security zone as long as Hezbollah has not been disarmed throughout Lebanon — and the threat to the residents of the north has not been removed," Katz said on X.
"We are pursuing a determined policy stipulating that any shooting or launch of drones and UAVs toward Israeli cities, moshavim, or kibbutzim will be met with a powerful response against the Dahiyeh district in Beirut," Katz added.
"If Hezbollah joins an Iranian attack on Israel, it will receive a harsh blow," Katz said.
Yemeni government forces intensified pressure on the Houthi stronghold of Taiz on Tuesday following a 24-hour offensive as part of "Operation Dawn Yemen."
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said 744 strikes hit "legitimate military targets," including fortifications, supply networks and command centers.
The military also reported that 200 Houthi fighters were "neutralized" and that 90 vehicles and key facilities were disabled.
Deputy White House press secretary Anna Kelly said Tuesday that the United States would not attack Iran ahead of the midterm elections.
Responding to a question about recent talks between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Kelly told Al Jazeera that, as Trump stated, “Iran is in very bad condition – both economically and militarily – and the blockade will remain in full force and effect with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait.”

articles.title_orig: China-US ocean freight rates hold steady as post-holiday space tightens
articles.title_zh: China-US ocean freight rates hold steady as post-holiday space tightens
articles.content_orig:
Mid-October 2026 saw the global trading landscape focus heavily on technical compliance and long-term litigation management, reports Freight Right , a freight forwarder and licensed customs broker based in Los Angeles. U.S. Customs and Border Protection launched Phase 3 of its automated CAPE portal to process remaining back-duty refunds from struck-down tariffs , even as the U.S, Court of International Trade froze pending Section 122 importer lawsuits while appellate courts review executive authority. Concurrently, cross-border supply chains operating under Washington's centralized trade architecture shifted attention to auto manufacturing, with industry leaders launching urgent campaigns in Detroit to avert a proposed 50% automotive tariff hike threatened for early 2027 .
China-U.S. Ocean Freight Market:
China to U.S. ocean freight rates remain unchanged week over week as carriers extend first-half October pricing. However, space has become harder to secure following China’s National Day holiday, making booking lead times and schedule reliability more pressing concerns.
CEA to USWC: Standard market rates are hovering around $8,000/FEU. However, secondary volume discount rates are available at $6,900 to $7,000/FEU for multi-container commitments. Rates have remained unchanged relative to the first half of the month.
CEA to USEC: Rates continue to hold in the $9,000+/FEU range. Special blended rates for higher-volume bookings are holding near $8,450/FEU. As with the West Coast, rates have shown no net increase or decrease week-over-week.
Freight Right’s Lowest Rate indicators are finding that importers can find spot rates as low as $6,400 from China to U.S. West Coast and $8,129 from China to U.S. East Coast.
[ Read more about the state of the ocean freight spot market with Freight Right’s TrueFreight Index. ]
Space constraints are expected to continue through the end of October as carriers clear holiday backlogs. Booking at least two weeks before the intended departure is increasingly necessary, though it does not guarantee space or prevent a rollover.
Rates could remain near current levels into November and December if carriers continue to control capacity, even without a substantial increase in demand. A further increase ahead of Chinese New Year is possible, but this week’s discussion does not confirm a new ocean rate increase.
For shippers, the immediate priority is building more time into shipment plans. Departure dates, terminal receiving windows, and transshipment connections remain subject to change. If a delay moves a container into a new pricing period, a future rate increase could also affect the final cost.
Paying the current market rate does not guarantee priority loading or an on-time departure. Confirm space, rate validity, and receiving dates before arranging container pickup, and allow additional time for shipments with firm delivery deadlines.
China to U.S. air freight rates rose sharply after the National Day holiday, reversing the usual seasonal pattern. Airlines typically offer lower prices during and immediately after the Oct. 1-7 break to fill space. This year, capacity remained tight during the holiday, and the market has seen two to three rounds of price increases since factories resumed work on Oct. 8.
CEA to USWC: Rates are trending higher, with further increases expected this week. The Week 41 sheet lists standard-density carton rates to LAX at approximately $5.85-$7.69 per kg, depending on origin and routing. Comparable SFO rates range from approximately $5.85-$6.77 per kg.
CEA to USEC: East Coast services face the same upward pressure. Standard-density carton rates to JFK range from approximately $6.88-$8 per kg, with direct Shanghai–JFK service at the upper end.
Based on this past week’s market report, upward rate pressure is expected to continue through the end of December. Reduced airline capacity, higher fuel costs, and growing technology shipments are coinciding with the traditional peak season for U.S.-bound exports.
Shippers should book early, confirm space alongside pricing, and budget for further increases. Direct and connecting services already show meaningful price differences, making routing flexibility useful where delivery schedules allow. Quotes should be reconfirmed before booking as airlines continue to adjust rates.
This story was produced by Freight Right and reviewed and distributed by Stacker .

articles.title_orig: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
articles.title_zh: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
articles.content_orig:
It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation.
The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded.
The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine.
Four forthcoming rockets all have engines built by the rocket’s manufacturer in the United States. Each of these companies has taken various lessons from SpaceX’s successful Falcon 9 rocket, arguably the most important of which is to build as much of one’s rocket, and particularly the engines, in-house as possible to control timelines and costs.
Now, with SpaceX pulling the Falcon 9 rocket from the commercial market as soon as 2028, the “race” to bring new medium-lift capacity into service is for more than bragging rights. There are fortunes to be made, and commercial space startups to be saved.
Satellite operators legitimately don’t know who to book launches with in the 2027 to 2030 timeframe because of uncertainty over which rockets will be available. The Falcon 9 is no longer for sale. The larger Vulcan and New Glenn rockets have stacked manifests and are expensive for small- and medium-sized satellites. And no one really knows which new medium-lift vehicles will be ready and capable of scaling up their launch cadence.
With all of this in mind, Ars Technica is here to help with a guide to the medium-lift space race in the United States, along with some (almost certainly wrong) predictions on when the rockets may debut. The list below is in our expected order of launch. Disagree? Feel free to shame us in the comments. And if you’re an engineer or technician working on one of these projects, keep going. This stuff is really hard and we salute your dedication. Prove us wrong!
The smallest of the medium-lift rockets under development, with a capacity of 3 tons in fully reusable mode and 7 tons in expendable mode, the Nova rocket is also arguably the most ambitious.
That’s because the rocket aims for full reusability, with a novel upper stage thruster design and heat shield to solve the difficult problem of protecting a vehicle reentering at orbital velocity. Additionally, the first-stage engines are full-flow staged combustion, which is ambitious for a first engine design.
Despite all of this, the rocket is making credible progress toward liftoff. The Nova rocket’s first stage is nearly complete at its factory in Kent, Washington. Last week Stoke shipped the second stage of Nova to its test site, and if hot-fire tests are successful it will move to the launch site. The launch complex at Cape Canaveral, Florida, is nearly complete.
Recently, for the first time, Stoke began to publicly talk about a date for Nova’s debut. The company is targeting “early” 2027 for launch. That’s probably optimistic, but we could see a late spring or summer debut.
Predicted launch debut : July 2027
Technically, this is not a medium-lift rocket. The company is advertising up to 33.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit in fully expendable mode for Terran R. But new rockets rarely hit their advertised lift capacity early in their lifetime, and with a reusable first stage (which is necessary for the economics of Terran R to close), the lift capacity is closer to 20 metric tons.
Nevertheless, this is a large and ambitious project. And it was pretty much left for dead until former Google Chief Executive Eric Schmitt acquired the company a year and a half ago. Schmitt has injected much-needed funding into Relativity, and sources report that morale at the Long Beach, California-based company has improved significantly.
In recent months the company has reported some notable progress. It completed acceptance testing for all 13 of the Aeon R engines that will power its first stage, qualified the first stage structures, and is making progress on assembly of the first stage. Then, last Friday, the company said the Terran R’s second stage had successfully completed its first integrated hot fire test.
Stoke and Relativity are fairly close to one another in their development timelines. Relativity is ahead in second stage testing, but Stoke has a lead in launch site readiness. I am going to give the slight edge to the smaller rocket in terms of being ready for launch.
Predicted launch debut : September 2027
With a lift capacity of between 8.5 and 15 metric tons, depending on first stage reuse and landing site, Rocket Lab’s Neutron rocket slots somewhere in between Nova and Terran R.
For a long time it appeared as though Neutron would become the first new medium-lift rocket to debut since Antares, but the vehicle has had some teething pains: Rocket Lab has experienced some problems with the Archimedes engine , and more recently the company revealed some challenges with carbon-fiber domes.
The Neutron rocket’s first stage is the “largest pressurized structure ever made out of carbon composite,” Rocket Lab chief Peter Beck said this month. “Because of its scale, we’ve had to develop new out-of-autoclave processes to build Neutron, and this includes custom cure cycles for the very large pieces, like the forward and aft domes for the propellant tanks on Stage One.”
That doesn’t sound particularly easy. Given the lack of flight hardware in evidence, we’re not sure the company meets its latest launch target, which is now sometime in 2027.
Predicted launch debut : January 2028
We began this article with the Antares rocket, which was developed by Orbital Sciences. That company was later acquired by Northrop Grumman. A few years ago, seeking a home-grown alternative to Antares, Northrop announced a partnership with Firefly to co-develop the Eclipse rocket .
Firefly is developing the Miranda engines that will power Eclipse’s first stage, and this work appears to be progressing well. But there has been little public talk about development of the first and second stage hardware that will be built around the Miranda engine. Similar to Rocket Lab, Firefly and Northrop are also working with carbon-composite structures, so there may be some challenges there.
The partnership between Firefly, a new space company, and Northrop, a traditional space company, is also likely to produce some friction. It is difficult to make an educated guess on Eclipse because there is so much uncertainty about the rocket’s development. Typically, that means things aren’t going well or quickly. For now, we’re leaning toward pessimism.
Predicted launch debut : NET 2029

articles.title_orig: Nigeria confirms an Ebola case, health minister says
articles.title_zh: Nigeria confirms an Ebola case, health minister says
articles.content_orig:
Nigeria has recorded a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda in East Africa to Abuja, capital of the West African state.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the diagnosis had been confirmed by laboratory tests.
The patient is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja.
Health authorities have begun contact-tracing to prevent further spread, with 44 close contacts of the woman identified.
Nigeria, the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East Africa, successfully stopped a previous outbreak in 2014.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports .
It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.
The disease has also spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.
On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.
Since the outbreak, Nigeria has stepped up disease surveillance, with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control issuing public health advice to travellers.
The agency says travellers from countries with active or relevant Ebola transmission may be required to complete a health declaration form. Those arriving from other countries are currently exempt.
It has also urged travellers to remain vigilant and seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms of Ebola.
In 2014, Nigeria managed to beat an outbreak of Ebola which caused at least eight deaths.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran lauds ties with Russia, contradicting Trump's claim of little Russian support for Tehran
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran lauds ties with Russia, contradicting Trump's claim of little Russian support for Tehran
articles.content_orig:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Tuesday that he visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying he "was there visiting our troops" and "had a chance to talk to the prime minister."
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
"Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about but they've been good partners and I appreciate that," Hegseth said of his meeting with Netanyahu.
U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.
The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.
"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.
"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."
The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it would not return to the negotiating table unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."
"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."
Iran is taking a hard-line stance on negotiations with the U.S. to end the war, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying Tuesday there will be no return to talks without a halt to the pressure campaign by the U.S.
Pezeshkian met with representatives from Pakistan, including army chief Asim Munir, on Tuesday. Pakistan has played an integral role as a mediator in peace talks between the U.S. and Iran, including the brief success of the Islamabad Memorandum in June.
"(Pezeshkian) told Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir that US warmongering lies behind regional tensions, including disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz," according to a readout of the meeting from the official Iranian government account on X . "He said Washington must lift its pressures, threats and sanctions before any negotiations."
Those conditions are unlikely to be agreed upon by the U.S., which has stepped up its sanctions , dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, over the past month. President Trump has said the economic pressure campaign has become the main strategy for ending the war.
Pezeshkian also met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Tuesday. Iran and Russia have become powerful allies.
Naval mines have halted three tankers attempting to travel the Strait of Hormuz via routes considered illegal by Tehran, Iranian Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday.
"Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," the Guards said in an earlier statement on their official Sepah News website.
The Guards later said in a statement carried by state TV that a third oil tanker "exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz."
The tanker "carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil, had deactivated all of its radar and navigation systems," the statement added.
Iranian forces have, since the outbreak of the Middle East war, repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern, U.S.-approved route close to the Omani coast.
President Trump has said on several occasions that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of all mines.

articles.title_orig: Nearly $1 million worth of rare Pokemon and sports cards stolen from FedEx truck in Orange County heist, police say
articles.title_zh: Nearly $1 million worth of rare Pokemon and sports cards stolen from FedEx truck in Orange County heist, police say
articles.content_orig:
SANTA ANA, Calif. (KABC) -- Nearly $1 million in rare trading cards, including highly valued Pokémon cards, were stolen from a FedEx truck parked near an Orange County business that authenticates and grades the collectible items, according to police.
The theft is the latest in a string of heists involving Pokémon cards, which have exponentially increased in value in recent years.
The Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement on Tuesday that the heist occurred on Oct. 13 outside the Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) office in Santa Ana.
The hundreds of stolen cards are estimated to be worth a total of $963,000, according to police.
"However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined," according to the Santa Ana police statement.
The cards belong to collectors from across the country who submitted them to the PSA to be authenticated and graded.
Two full pallets of collectible cards were stolen, and some cards on a third pallet were also swiped when thieves broke into a FedEx truck, according to police.
"The pallets contained various trading cards, including, but not limited to, sports cards and Pokémon cards," according to the police statement.
Thieves carve hole through drywall to steal high-value Pokémon cards from Anaheim shop
As of Tuesday, no arrests have been announced in the memorabilia rip-off. Police said the investigation is ongoing.
The theft was first reported by The Athletic, which cited police sources saying the the FedEx truck was broken into during the 60 to 90 minutes the driver was away from the parked vehicle.
"We are aware of a theft involving a third-party shipping vehicle carrying PSA-graded items. We are working closely with law enforcement and the carrier as the investigation continues," Collectors, the parent company of PSA, said in a statement to ABC News.
The company said it deactivated the certificates for the missing cards and has notified its "marketplace partners to be on the lookout for rare and serialized items."
"Our customer service team has contacted affected customers directly and is arranging compensation based on fair market value," the company said. "We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset."
FedEx released a statement to ABC7, saying, "The security of our customers' shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation. Further questions should be referred to local investigators."
One victimized collector, known by his online handle, Sky-B Cards, issued a YouTube video statement , saying the 104 cards he submitted to PSA for grading were among the stolen items. He said he paid more than $8,000 to have the cards graded by PSA and that his cards were insured for more than $150,000.
"These were 104 cards that I've accumulated over two years," Sky-B Cards said in the YouTube video. "There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again, and honestly that's what hurts the most, outside of being absolutely financially destroyed here."
The heist is the latest in a string of thefts in Southern California and elsewhere in the country of highly valued Pokémon cards, highlighting what appears to be an ever-growing demand for merchandise from the popular childhood card game.
In February, thieves broke into a collectibles shop in Anaheim, by cutting a hole through the wall from a neighboring shop they also broke into, stealing tens of thousands of dollars worth of Pokémon cards.
Captured on video surveillance cameras, the three thieves were seen grabbing hundreds of trading cards and bolting from the shop in less than 10 minutes.
In April, thieves staged a smash-and-grab heist at Elite Sports Cards in Chicago, stealing $100,000 in Pokémon cards, the store owner told ABC Chicago station WLS.
In an interview in April, Jared Mast, president of Mast Wealth Management Group, which deals in alternative investments including collectibles like Pokémon cards, told ABC News the value of Pokémon cards has risen sharply in the past year.
"I would say, collectively, over the last 12 months, things have gone up anywhere from 200 to 300%," Mast said.
Mast explained that Pokémon card value has risen in three different waves over the last decade. First, in 2016, with the arrival of Pokémon Go, the popular mobile game based on the playing cards, and then again in 2019 and 2020, as a generation of celebrities like Logan Paul invested in the collectibles.
ABC News contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: GLP-1 injections recalled nationwide. See affected products
articles.title_zh: GLP-1 injections recalled nationwide. See affected products
articles.content_orig:
The company received an FDA warning letter in December 2025 citing deficiencies in how it makes sterile drug products
ruizluquepaz / Getty Images
Apothecary Pharma LLC of Cary, North Carolina, is recalling 22 vials of tirzepatide injection across the U.S. because of a lack of assurance of sterility, according to the FDA. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The company started the voluntary recall on Sept. 24 and notified customers by letter, the FDA said. The agency classified the recall as Class II on Oct. 8, and it remains ongoing. The FDA did not issue a press release for the recall.
The recalled product is Apothecary Pharma tirzepatide injection, 18 mg/mL, in 4 mL multi-dose vials. Lot numbers run from AP-202622 to AP-202644, with beyond-use dates between Oct. 7 and Nov. 26, according to USA Today .
The recall also covers one vial of Apothecary NAD+ injection, 200 mg/mL, in a 6 mL multi-dose vial, lot AP-202647. The FDA gave it the same Class II classification and the same reason for recall.
Class II applies to products whose use may lead to short-term or correctable health problems, though serious harm is unlikely, according to USA Today.
The FDA sent Apothecary Pharma a warning letter in December 2025 that listed several violations. They included "serious deficiencies in your practices for producing drug products intended or expected to be sterile, which put patients at risk," according to USA Today. Neither the company nor the FDA responded to USA Today's Oct. 19 requests for comment, according to USA Today.
Neither the FDA nor Apothecary Pharma has publicly said how the vials involved should be handled, according to USA Today. USA Today advised patients with an affected lot to stop using it and to contact their prescriber.
The FDA has warned patients away from compounded versions of weight loss drugs , saying they should be used only when a patient's medical needs cannot be met by an approved medication. In June, the agency issued 25 warning letters to telehealth companies over what it characterized as inaccurate or deceptive marketing of compounded weight loss drugs.
Many compounders kept making versions of tirzepatide and semaglutide even after the FDA took both off its list of drugs in short supply, a change that came in stages from late 2024 into early 2025, according to USA Today.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft reportedly plans Xbox handheld in 2027, next-gen console in 2028
articles.title_zh: Microsoft reportedly plans Xbox handheld in 2027, next-gen console in 2028
articles.content_orig:
The next Xbox could cost between $1,200 and $1,800 if Microsoft doesn’t subsidize it.
The next Xbox could cost between $1,200 and $1,800 if Microsoft doesn’t subsidize it.
Microsoft is reportedly planning to launch an Xbox “next-generation handheld device” for the holiday season of 2027. The Xbox next-gen console, codename Project Helix, would then launch in the holidays of 2028, according to a new report from Fortune .
The report doesn’t make it clear whether the handheld would be made by a manufacturer like Asus, or by Microsoft itself. Xbox teamed up with Asus for its Xbox Ally devices, which ran a modified version of Windows 11 with an Xbox mode enabled. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has also described Project Helix as a “ family of devices ,” suggesting that Microsoft’s next Xbox console may not be just one piece of hardware.
Last year Microsoft and AMD announced a “strategic multi-year partnership” to work together on “a portfolio of devices,” including Microsoft’s next-generation console. It seems increasingly likely that this will include a range of “Xbox” devices, running on AMD’s new chips.
The regular next-generation Xbox console may not arrive until 2028, though. Fortune reports that Microsoft is currently projecting that its Xbox Project Helix console may cost “between $1,200 to $1,800” for consumers, unless Microsoft is willing to subsidize the cost of the hardware.
Microsoft’s Windows and Xbox teams have also reportedly clashed over what software will power the next-gen Xbox. That’s not terribly surprising given the two teams have clashed multiple times over the past 25 years of Xbox. It sounds like Xbox is now controlling the direction of the software on Helix, though.
The report also touches on the rumored changes to Xbox Game Pass. Last month rumors emerged that Microsoft was working on an overhaul to Game Pass that will create tiers with or without ads, much like Netflix and other streaming services. Fortune says Xbox is looking at including add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer. This would make Game Pass a lot more flexible, but it’s not clear what happens to day one games and the overall price of Game Pass.
One of Sharma’s first big moves as Xbox CEO was reversing the Game Pass price hikes , after she admitted internally that “Game Pass has become too expensive for players.” Xbox dropped future Call of Duty titles from day one on Game Pass, and brought prices back down for its subscription service.
Fortune also reports that Sharma is planning a fresh round of Xbox layoffs this month, followed by more in November and January.

articles.title_orig: US to approve Boeing 737 Max 10 for passenger service after years of delays, AP source says
articles.title_zh: US to approve Boeing 737 Max 10 for passenger service after years of delays, AP source says
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration on Tuesday signed off on the Boeing 737 Max 10 after years of delays , a major win for the manufacturer and the last in Boeing's best-selling family of jets to get government approval.
The green light comes weeks after federal officials reviewed a navigation system glitch on the aircraft but deemed it was not a safety-of-flight issue.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC's Phil LeBeau that safety is paramount, but he also said the U.S. needs to improve its certification process.
"It takes Boeing, to certify an aircraft in Europe, about half the time, less than half the time that it does in the U.S. You have China now playing to take over in aviation," Duffy said. "We have to certify aircraft more quickly if we're going to compete as Americans."
The 737 Max 10, the largest model in the family that can seat up to 230 people, was set to start flying in 2020, but increased scrutiny following two Max crashes in 2018 and 2019 and other safety issues delayed its certification. Engineering changes were also required, including to an anti-icing system for the aircraft's engines.
Max 10 customers include Alaska Airlines , American Airlines , United Airlines and Delta Air Lines . Boeing said the Max 10 makes up about 30% of its Max backlog.
Airlines can finally start flying passengers soon after planes are certified, but it can take months for carriers to work them into schedules.
"Completing the certification program clears the path for us to deliver a Boeing airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation," Stephanie Pope, CEO of Boeing's commercial airplane unit, said in a news release.
United CEO Scott Kirby told CNBC in August that the airline had been waiting so long for the Max 10 that the lie-flat seats it expected for the plane no longer make sense and are sitting in a warehouse. Alaska Airlines last month said it plans to put lie-flat seats on some of its 737 Max 10s in a push for more premium offerings.
The FAA approved the smallest model of the 737 Max family, the Max 7 , in early August.
Boeing has been working to ramp up production of its 737 Maxes and 787 Dreamliners, which are key to its recovery since airlines and other customers pay the bulk of the aircraft's price upon delivery. The manufacturer opened a fourth production line in Everett, Washington, in July for its 737 Max airplanes.

On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs.
PyTorch is the popular open-source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.
Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps.
Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default.
Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.
Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite , to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.
None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

articles.title_orig: Delivery Robots Accused Of Scanning Customers’ Faces, Sharing Biometric Data
articles.title_zh: Delivery Robots Accused Of Scanning Customers’ Faces, Sharing Biometric Data
articles.content_orig:
The battle over Chicago’s food delivery robots has reached the courts, with two customers accusing the companies behind them of collecting their biometric data without consent.
The men filed separate class-action lawsuits in Cook County court Oct. 9 against Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics, alleging the companies violated a state privacy law. They claim the companies’ machines scanned their faces and hands without their knowledge or consent.
Both companies dispute the allegations.
The lawsuits allege the robots’ cameras and LiDAR — a technology that sends out laser pulses to measure distances and map the surrounding environment — captured measurements of customers’ faces and hands as they approached the machines to retrieve their orders.
Mitchell Breidinger says he ordered groceries through DoorDash in September 2025 and never chose robot delivery. But his order was assigned to a Coco robot, according to his lawsuit. When it arrived, he had to stand close to the machine to enter a code and retrieve his groceries.
Breidinger alleges the robot’s cameras recorded his face, head and hands, while its LiDAR sensors measured their geometry. His lawsuit also alleges a remote operator watched video of the delivery in real time. He says Coco did not tell him in writing that it would collect his biometric information, explain how long it would keep the data or obtain his written consent.
Barry Schain alleges a similar experience with Serve Robotics. He says he has received three deliveries from Serve robots, most recently Oct. 4, when an Uber Eats order was assigned to a robot even though he had not selected robot delivery, according to the lawsuit.
Both lawsuits claim the companies retain video and sensor data to train artificial intelligence systems. Schain’s lawsuit also points to Serve’s disclosures about licensing video and LiDAR datasets to third parties for AI training. Breidinger’s lawsuit claims Coco has shared robot-collected data with OpenAI and other third parties.
Customers’ biometric measurements are then stored alongside their names and addresses in the companies’ data systems, according to the lawsuits, linking the data to identifiable individuals.
The lawsuits accuse the companies of violating the Illinois Biometric Privacy Act, which requires companies collecting biometric data to provide written notice explaining what they collect and why, obtain written consent and maintain a policy for retaining and destroying the data.
Spokespersons for both Coco and Serve denied that the companies collect biometric information from customers or passersby. A Serve spokesperson said the company “will defend against” the lawsuit, while a Coco spokesperson said the company is “confident that this frivolous lawsuit will go away.”
“This lawsuit fundamentally misunderstands our technology, we have not collected biometric data in Chicago,” the Coco spokesperson said in a statement, adding that complying with privacy laws is a “top priority” for the company.
“The data we share is navigational data used to make sidewalks safer for all users,” the Coco spokesperson continued. “For example, we provide real-time sidewalk hazard information to BlindSquare, a navigation app built for people who are blind or have low vision. We do not share data from the beginning or end of delivery trips under our data sharing partnerships. Privacy and compliance with the law are top priorities in everything we do.”
The Serve spokesperson said the company’s robots use cameras and sensors to navigate sidewalks safely.
“Serve does not use that data to identify individuals and our systems are not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
The lawsuits seek statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation or $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation, as well as other relief.
The lawsuits add to growing scrutiny of delivery robots that have become a regular sight on Chicago sidewalks, where residents have raised concerns about safety, accessibility, surveillance and the potential loss of delivery jobs.
Chicago launched its delivery robot pilot program in 2022 under former Mayor Lori Lightfoot. Coco began operating in the city in late 2024, followed by Serve Robotics in September 2025. The program, overseen by the Chicago Department of Transportation and the Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection, is set to expire in May 2027 unless the City Council approves an extension.
Resident Josh Robertson started a petition last year calling on the city to pause the program until officials release safety and accessibility data, hold a public hearing and establish clearer rules. More than 4,500 people had signed the petition as of last month. Residents have reported robots blocking sidewalks and crosswalks, creating obstacles for people with disabilities and raising concerns about cameras recording pedestrians.
The pushback has also reached City Hall. Ald. Daniel La Spata (1st) rejected plans to expand the robots across much of his ward in February after more than 83 percent of residents who responded to an online survey strongly opposed the expansion.
The city has also created a 311 category for residents to report safety concerns and other complaints about the devices.
In March, a Serve robot smashed through the glass of a Chicago Transit Authority bus shelter in West Town, scattering shards of glass across the sidewalk. Days later, a Coco robot collided with another bus shelter in Old Town. Both companies said they were investigating the crashes and took responsibility for repair costs.
In September, a video showing more than a dozen Coco robots apparently circling one another and getting stuck on a Chicago sidewalk went viral, drawing hundreds of thousands of views and renewing criticism of the technology.
The companies have defended the robots as a safer, more sustainable option for short-distance deliveries that can reduce car trips and traffic congestion.
